statement_paraphrased: Emissions of the iron-and-steel industry 2005-2013 follow the economy (up in period 1, down in period 2); DEHSt states that no clear, significant trend towards lower emission intensity can be derived so far.

On a consistent-scope basis (estimated pre-2013 emissions of later-added processing plants and installations no longer in the ETS included) emissions of the iron-and-steel industry were about 2 percent higher in 2017 than in 2005.

Emissions rose from 2013 to 2018 (except 2016); 2019 is slightly below 2013; versus 2005 total emissions are 9 percent lower in 2019 (same consistent-scope basis). Text says 35.5 Mt for 2019, the table says 35,577 kt.

German iron-and-steel emissions rose to 2018 above 2013 although German crude steel output was flat (42.6 Mt in 2013, 42.4 Mt in 2018) and EU output was flat; DEHSt says production trends give no plausible explanation.

Blast-furnace (oxygen steel) route dominates: about 84 percent of the sector emissions for about 70 percent of crude steel; electric steel about 30 percent of output but under 3 percent of the sector emissions (direct emissions only; indirect power emissions are higher for EAF).
2023: iron-and-steel emissions -2 percent vs 2022; oxygen-steel output -0.9 percent, electric steel -10.8 percent (WV Stahl).
2024: oxygen-steel output a little over +3 percent, electric steel +10.2 percent (WV Stahl); emissions of the sector about +2 percent.

2025: industrial ETS installations -5.5 percent to about 97 Mt; clear decreases in iron and steel among others, mainly production-driven; UBA says ramp-up of direct reduction and related infrastructure is not yet fast enough.
